newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish pork industry urges EU concessions to USA.
newsitem.headline: Danish pork industry urges EU concessions to USA.

text.p: Denmark's pork industry, fearing dwindling earnings and fewer jobs if a feared U.S.- Europe meat trade war goes ahead, appealed on Thursday for the European Union to soften its stand on U.S. poultry imports.
"We intensively encourage the parties to show flexibility in the coming two weeks' negotiations," a statement by the Danish Bacon and Meat Council said.
"Especially we encourage the Danish Minister of Food, Agriculture and Fisheries to strengthen his contribution toward the EU system concerning a softening of the EU attitude."
The responsible ministry official could not be reached for comment.

Bacon and Meat Council spokesman Niels Christian Joergensen said that a U.S. ban on EU meat imports, mainly Danish spare ribs and canned ham, would cost the industry about 350 million crowns ($54.9 million) a year and 200 jobs.
"The majority of the products we are selling in the United States, mainly barbecue specialities, are very difficult to sell on other markets, at least at the same price," he told Reuters.

"It's not a tradition in Europe to eat these bone products and therefore alternative export possibilities are limited. My guess is that some of the spare ribs would be sold for pet food production," he said.

Total Danish pork exports to the United States were worth about one billion crowns a year he said, around five percent of the Danish pork industry's total exports, 65-70 percent of which were to partner countries in the 15-nation EU.
Overall Danish exports totalled 283.5 billion crowns in 1996, National Statistics Office data shows.
The U.S. meat sales came under threat this week when the EU and United States failed to agree on equivalent standards for veterinary inspection of meat and poultry products.
An agreement would allow each side to accept meat and poultry from the other even if inspection methods differ.

On Tuesday, Brussels announced it was implementing new standards throughout the EU that would tighten controls on incoming U.S. poultry shipments. Washington responded by requiring European meat and poultry plants to meet U.S. inspection standards by April 15 or they would not be able to export to the United States.
The two sides are planning to continue talks next week in a last ditch effort to avert a trade war.
The European Commission said on Wednesday that it did not intend to escalate the conflict, but saw little room for manoeuvre. --Copenhagen newsroom +45 33969650 ($ = 6.372 Danish Crowns)
